utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please proceed to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. And this is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances -- wait. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls, and good afternoon to you both. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic. May I expand my remarks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. And good afternoon to you first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would like first of all to -- we may finish today. And the reason I'm saying that -- what I'm going to say is because of that. I will probably file a motion tomorrow which might require a sitting sometime next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so I just wanted to make you and the Prosecutor aware of that. And in addition, I would ask again your indulgence while I go forth and work on Prijedor and leave Mr. Trbojevic in charge of matters here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's no problem. May we have an indication what kind of motion we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to say very much about it because I don't want to make any mistakes, but it will have to do with a number of things, including Rule 68, the Prijedor case, and the military documents. It refers to all three of those matters, I think. It's in its very early rough draft stages and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come to it when it's been filed. So I think we can proceed. Usher -- where's the usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have one very brief preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The motion on behalf of Jonathan Randal for release of transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have been informed about it by my ALO, but it has not yet arrived on my desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, just to say we have no objection and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have no objection. Yes, Mr. Ackerman has left anyway. I would imagine that he has no objection. Mr. Trbojevic, this is a motion by Mr. Jonathan Randal to have a copy of the transcripts which relate to his case, if I may say so. Do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours, that Mr. Ackerman insisted on the cross-examination of Mr. Randal; if such a ruling is made, that he be brought here to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's -- that's -- I don't think you understood me or I -- what I said was not translated properly. I don't know; either of the two. You know that last week we discussed what's happened in the appeal, and we had a debate here which lasted for hours. What Mr. Randal wants is a copy of the transcript of the debate in this chamber of last week, so that he can come to no -- he will be made aware of what was said here with regard to his case. And that's because it was in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me if I have any objections, I have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So then we can actually proceed by giving an oral decision here and now that the motion is granted, there being no objection from either the Prosecution or the Defence. All right? Granted as requested. Usher, please, the witness. Thank you for your cooperation, Mr. Trbojevic and Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Ticevic. We will continue and finish with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But before we do so, may I kindly ask you to repeat your solemn declaration, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have a seat. Sir, before we continue, there's one very simple point from yesterday that I want to clear up so there's no ambiguity in the transcript. You stated that the person who gave you orders and told you what you would do each day as regards the work obligation you performed after your release from the school was Ratko Marcetic, and you stated that he was a sergeant that you would meet at the checkpoint every morning. He was a sergeant in the military or in the police?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a sergeant in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday when we left off, we were looking at a Kljuc report of the CSB, signed by Chief Vinko Kondic, in which he explained that he and the police were not filing reports against known perpetrators of serious crimes against the Muslim population, including murders, because it would not be advisable due to the current political situation and pressure from the international community. Do you remember us talking about that?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1045. You'd also just finished telling us about the investigation, such as it was, into the murder which you witnessed, or you were present for, of Ibrahim Kumalic and Draganovic. My question is, having read to you this section of the report: In your case, the crime which you witnessed, did you feel as though there was any serious investigation being made into those two murders?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no serious investigation. Two military policemen came, they took notes, and left. No official person was present, apart from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just if you know - I don't know whether you do or not - was there ever a prosecution in that case, to your knowledge, of those men who you were warned not to identify?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no investigation, and they're living in freedom to this day, wherever they're living.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I'm correct, it was shortly after these murders which took place at the house you were living at that you decided to leave Kljuc; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you some questions about the actual process of leaving Kljuc at that time for you and for other people who were trying Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If the witness could please see P989.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We've looked at this exhibit before. It's the book of minutes from the Kljuc Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff. And I'll ask you to look at the minutes from the 9th of June session, 1992, which began on page 14 of the English translation, and if I have it right, on the page with the ERN 00573870 in the B/C/S original. Have you found that section, sir? It's headed "Minutes from the Kljuc SO Crisis Staff session, 9th of June, 1992," and the first heading is "Agenda."

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you answer verbally for the record, please. You've shaken your head to indicate yes, but could you answer whether you've found that section.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if we look under "Agenda," item 3 on the agenda at this Kljuc Crisis Staff session is "Report from the session of the Banja Luka Regional Crisis Staff." And if you turn the page, we can see item 3, where Veljko Kondic, it states: "Informed the Crisis Staff of the conclusions of the Regional Crisis Staff session and remarked on the most important issues." On the next page, if you could just read down what those important issues were. And you can stop at -- just above where it says that, "Muslim and Croatian personnel should be removed from the most responsible posts in the army and police ranks." Just read down to that section. And do you see where, just above that section, one of the important issues which the Kljuc Crisis Staff was being briefed on was that the question of population resettlement should be solved and that an agency, a team of men, should be formed to work on this issue? Have you found that? It's the third item under item 3.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3, Kondic Veljko; is that correct what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look below there, the third bulleted point concerns the question of population resettlement.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just confirm in the original before you, does that point state that: "The question of population resettlement should be solved and that an agency (a team of men) should be formed to work on this issue"?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, what page does the witness have in front of him? [Microphone not activated] Just give me the last four numbers. THE USHER: 871.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it, but I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. So Mr. Nicholls, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please turn on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ticevic, I'd just like you to confirm if it's accurate that in the original it states that: "The question of population resettlement should be solved and that an agency (a team of men) should be formed to work on this issue."

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That's the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if the witness could now please be shown P240 before I ask him the question. Sorry, this was not on the list, Your Honours, but I've passed it out. It was a Banja Luka exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the following: Could the Prosecutor put his question related to what is stated in these minutes. The question to the witness was whether that is stated in the minutes, but he didn't go on to put a question to the witness about those minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm planning to do that, Your Honours. I think it's clearer if these two exhibits are read together, and then I'll ask him my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Otherwise, I'll just ask the question twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll come to your objection after seeing what this other document is all about and then seeing what the question is. Yes, P240. Put the English version on the ELMO, please, and the B/C/S you hand to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is a document from the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, dated the 12th of June, 1992, and it's to the chiefs of all public security stations. It refers to: "The Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina has adopted the following decision." And that decision was dated June 10th, 1992. So this -- Mr. Ticevic, this decision is being forwarded. The decision of the Crisis Staff -- under section 1, 10th of June, states: "Only children, women, and old people may voluntarily, that is, of their own free will, leave the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Is that stated under Roman numeral I in your B/C/S original?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then at the very end, the last paragraph of this document, it states: "You are to brief the staff of your public security station about this decision and arrange for the required cooperation with the humanitarian organisations in your area for its implementation." Signed, Stojan Zupljanin. My question is: You stated yesterday that, in the beginning, only women and children and the elderly were allowed to leave, or you stated that men of military age, rather, were not allowed to leave. You've seen these documents from the 9th, 10th, and 12th of June referring to that issue, prohibiting men of military age from leaving the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You, however, were able to leave in September. If you know, when were men of military age able to begin to freely leave Kljuc municipality between June and September?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. At first it was women, children, the sick, the disabled who left. I left at the end of September because, according to the assessment of the JNA, actually a major who was my commander in the barracks, he proclaimed me mentally immature; however, many men who were able-bodied never left, because those remained to do work obligations and we found them there when we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on. When you did leave in September, did you have a house and any property in Kljuc at that time? You said that you left with nothing yesterday, but I'm wondering if you had any property that you left behind.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a house together with my brother in Pudin Han.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was actually your brother's house, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house was my brother's, but I lived in it, and he's living in Switzerland, so we lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you have to sign any documents in order to be able to leave Kljuc in September; any official documents?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. First of all, meet all our debts towards Republika Srpska, electricity and things like that. After that, we all had to sign a document leaving all our mobile and immobile property voluntarily to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, you said "we." Did you personally have to sign all of these documents?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I signed one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1007, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what you're being shown is entitled "Kljuc Municipal Assembly War Presidency Decision," which was adopted at a meeting held on the 30th Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of July, 1992. It's the decision on the criteria for the possibility to move out of the territory of Kljuc municipality. Could you just read to yourself Article 1 and tell me when you've read that.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this Article 1 states that one of the conditions stipulated by the decision was, to paraphrase, people who wish to leave are allowed to move out voluntarily and permanently from the territory of Kljuc municipality. Do you have to sign that you were moving out voluntarily and also permanently?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have to sign that. But we also had to sign that we were going to third countries, that we would not become members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could you please just read to yourself the next article, Article 2. And this Article concerns what happens to immovable property, real estate, real property, to persons who are choosing to permanently leave the municipality of Kljuc. And it states that: "The exchange of immovable property must be carried out before or at the latest within three months of the departure or Kljuc municipality shall seize the property in question." That's an exchange with somebody from outside the municipality. Or 2: "Persons who leave their immovable property at the disposal of Kljuc municipality shall also be allowed to leave the territory of Kljuc municipality permanently." Finally: "The sale of immovable property is not allowed." My question is, once you've read that: Which option occurred with your brother's house? Did he leave it to the municipality? Did he exchange it with a family that was trying to come to Kljuc? Or did he just abandon it?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother was not there, as I have said. He's been living in Switzerland for a long time. But I had to sign that I was leaving the house and everything in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember - if you don't remember, that's fine - do you remember who you signed that you were leaving the house to? Who took possession of the house when you left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those are two questions, Mr. Nicholls. Let's go through them one after the other, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, when you left and you signed that document, did you -- first of all, did you sign a document turning over the house, leaving the house that your brother owned?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did sign a document in Tihomir Dakic's office, a highly-ranked politician of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And within -- if it's -- did it state within the document you signed who was now the legal owner of the house once you had signed that document?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But they gave us a sort of ultimatum. The deadline was three months for an exchange, and it was impossible to do it in that time, so I signed something like this: I, my name, my father's name, am leaving all my immovable property to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, can you briefly tell the Court what -- how you physically left. On the day you left, where did you go? Did you board a bus or a train? How did you actually physically come to leave the municipality, and who transported you out, if it was any organisation?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that I don't wish to name the person who helped me, for his own safety. I travelled by bus, like other people. And there were a lot of people inside. It was crammed full. It was stuffy. But this friend of mine - again he was a highly-ranked officer - said to a civilian policeman that I had to reach my destination and that nothing could be allowed to happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, is that one bus -- you were obviously on a bus, but was that bus part of a convoy of buses, or was it a bus -- a single bus that was leaving?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 14 buses, something like that, and several trucks with trailers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. [Microphone not activated] Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you personally see, before you left, any other convoys like this, of buses taking civilians out of Kljuc, permanently leaving Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several convoys that left before I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when people like yourself boarded these convoys to leave, was there any set procedure or any names checked off? Were there any final forms to fill out, or did you just -- how did you know when to appear and which bus you were going to get on, and on what day you were going to leave?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were informed that at 9.00 - I don't remember the date - should be in front of the youth centre in Kljuc. And once we got there and as we boarded the buses, we left behind more valuable things, and the names were called out from a list of people who had paid, and we boarded the buses one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you have to, in addition to these official forms and paying off all bills and debts, did you have to pay any bribes to be allowed onto this convoy? Did you have to pay any individuals? Put it that way.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not, but some people did. They would leave their tractors behind or a cow or something to somebody who could help them take care of their paperwork.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1059, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, you looked at this document yesterday as well. This is a 16th of February, 1993 report to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps Banja Luka from Colonel Gojko Vujnovic. Sorry, it's authored by Assistant Commander for Civilian Affairs Slobodan Dakic. And I'll ask you to find the section entitled "Departure of the Muslims in the period from May 1992 to 31st of January, 1993," which is probably on page 4 of the original.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You stated in your statement to the OTP that by the time you left, you estimated that about 90 per cent of the non-Serbs had left Kljuc, either forcibly or under duress. I'd like you to just look at the figures contained in this report to the 1st Krajina Corps. "Out of 4.200 residents of the Sanica local commune, 4.154 people left and 46 remained. Most of those who stayed are sickly elderly people with low incomes." Next: "Out of 3.649 residents of the Velagici local commune, 3.429 left and about 220 remained. Lists indicate that for those remaining --" it's not clear from the translation, that -- destinations, it appears, for those remaining families, people, have already been drafted. And it continues, if you read down through these yourself, to the Kljuc local commune: Out of 4.516 residents, only 884 remained. Do you agree with those figures, that those are accurate?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you know, what percentage of the population of Pudin Han remained by the time you left in September?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that about 10 per cent stayed. And it states also here in the documents that low income or poorer people stayed behind, those who could not meet their outstanding debts and pay for the trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. That means that the Prosecution has finished its questioning of you. Now it's the turn of the Defence to cross-examine you, and you will be cross-examined by the co-counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin, Mr. Milan Trbojevic. As I explained to you yesterday, your duty in answering Mr. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Trbojevic is exactly the same as when you were answering questions from the Prosecution. You have a duty and responsibility to answer each and every question truthfully and accurately unless we tell you not to answer it. Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ticevic, I will have to go back to the beginning now, so could you please pay attention because we will be starting from the very beginning of your testimony. In the statement you provided to the Prosecution and in the course of the examination here in the courtroom, you mentioned several uniforms. Yesterday you said, for example, that you saw people in military uniforms and in police uniforms come out of the Tamic van, truck. They were also wearing camouflage uniforms and some had red berets. If you agree, the term Tamic in Bosnia means a small truck or a small van. Isn't it a bit much to have four different kinds of uniforms come out of a Tamic?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I said from a Tamic -- from Tamics, which means that it wasn't one of such trucks but there were several such trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It was a misunderstanding. Were there any soldiers who were -- belonged to the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them personally not then, but I saw White Eagles and also Red Berets who said that they had come to separate the two sides hat were quarrelling. But however, we knew who they were and what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you provided to the Prosecution, you said that you heard that the Red Berets were from Pozarevac or Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally know who was the commander of the Red Berets because I worked in a cafe where they used to come by. It was a person called Frenki Stamatovic. I'm not sure what his last name is, but Frenki was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to dispute that. I'm just asking you whether you were sure they were from those towns.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them I considered as my friends before the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So you are sure that they are from Pozarevac and Pancevo and not from this area where you're from.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them are from Leskovac as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were a courier, that you would bring information to Mr. Omer Filipovic from Pudin Han. Did you just bring information from Pudin Han, or did you also return with information from Omer Filipovic to Pudin Han?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was according to need. If some relations were disrupted, I would then convey the message to Omer Filipovic that they would hold out until the negotiations or the talks were completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had attended certain meetings that were held which were headed by Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there was a mistake in interpretation but I said that they were mostly gatherings in local restaurants, and we trusted this man. They were not formal meetings, but it was just conversation about the political situation, because we felt a lot of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But you said that you had confidence in him because he was the legally elected president.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We gave him our votes, and I did have confidence in him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not disputing whether you should have had confidence in him or not. I'm just trying to establish his post.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic was the number one person in Kljuc. How shall I put it? He was the president of the Muslim Bosniak organisation, and Mr. Egrlic was the president of the SDA. However, from the top of the state, I think it came down from up above that Mr. Omer Filipovic should be the one to represent our side, to represent the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, those meetings where you had those confidential conversations, were they attended by Mr. Asim Egrlic, Amir Avdic, Esad Bender, Ismet Muratagic, Aziz Gromlic?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that these were not meetings with an agenda, they were informal meetings, and I never saw all of those people together at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You never saw Omer Filipovic and Asim Egrlic together.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but not at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Asim Egrlic travelled to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: He said that he went over there to take some money which was to be used to obtain weapons.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that money was sent in order to help families. I had family there and I sent money there. Those in Kljuc looked for any kind of document in order to accuse those people and to create propaganda and in order to cause a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But some weapons did come.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not something that I know. There is a person who has four sons in Switzerland and who was building a house before the war and he used to receive this money from Switzerland through some people. This person was also taken to the camp and accused of purchasing weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see an automatic rifle, which was quite unusual for Bosnia, in the possession of Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic was not a person with weapons. He was unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now remember for us the first, let's say, drastic events. As far as I understood from your testimony, on the 26th of May, you were in Pudin Han when shots were fired at a truck and a bus.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that's the correct date, but yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you provided to the Prosecution, you said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, just for the record, I think yesterday he said 27th of May was the date I put to him. So I don't know if it's a translation or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Agius, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I quite remember vividly that yesterday he did say 27th of May and not 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not insisting on the date. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, then. And your question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had just started stating, "In the statement that you provided to the Prosecution you said that --" and then you were going to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution, you said that there were from 200 to 300 people on both sides of the road. Yesterday you said perhaps there were even 400. I am asking you: Did any of those people whom I mentioned a little while ago for whom you said that you knew them but who did not attend these meetings, did any of those people -- were any of those people present at the time; Bender, Avdic, Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was on the 27th. You said it was the 26th. That's why I said I don't know. Number two, none of them was present. I provided a rough estimate the first time, 300, but I did say that there were women and children there, and they were also afraid, so I included them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to check whether any of them was present. Of course it's not possible to know the exact number, and I'm not trying to dispute that or precisely establish the number of people there. You told us that on the 27th of May a meeting was held between Vinko Kondic and Omer Filipovic and that you attended this meeting. The meeting was in Pudin Han, and that that was when Kondic issued an ultimatum for weapons to be handed over.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe it was a mistake in the translation, but this meeting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was held on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, the date is not that important, but was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Does that meeting have anything to do with the death of the police commander Stojakovic and the wounding of the two police officers?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting does have something to do with that. They wanted those who committed that to be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which number, Mr. Trbojevic? Exhibit number ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P921.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You saw this document before.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it, but I didn't read it. I would like to read the document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff, in the form of an order, even though it's wrong, but it says under point 1: "Calling all citizens who own illegally acquired weapons to hand them over..." and so on. It says "citizens." It does not state their nationality; isn't that right? Their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does say that, but it related to non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In item 2, it says: "Members of the Muslim nationality are ordered from the Ramici and Krasulje areas to hand over those responsible for yesterday's crime against the deputy commander of the police station."

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So the Muslim population here is explicitly being asked to hand over those responsible.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to state that the village of Ramici has nothing to do with that incident. There was only -- they were only looking for a reason to attack that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 states: "The body is being asked for"; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Item 4 states that "Citizens of Muslim nationality from the Egrlic and Pudin Han areas are asked to hand over those responsible for the attack on unarmed soldiers who were in an organised transport from Knin to Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those soldiers were not unarmed in that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So something is being asked for in those three paragraphs from Muslim -- citizens of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you, sir, please look at the deadline for handing over -- for the citizens in all of those 15 local communities; two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: They're indicated or termed under a general term "citizens."

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this pertains to non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were present there, could you please tell us how it came about that there was this shooting at the police officers.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present when there was shooting, when shots were fired at the police officers but at the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how those soldiers were arrested in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. There were no soldiers in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Those in the Red Berets [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the convoy. You are confusing those two things. The convoy was in Pudin Han and Crljeni, 20 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers were arrested in Crljeni? They were coming back from the front. Seven of them.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note that Crljeni are completely different, in a completely opposite side from my village. They are about 10 or 15 kilometres away from Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you if you know.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in line 24, Red Berets are mentioned in my question but no mention of Red Berets was made. I had said the name of the village Crljeni. Just the first two letters are similar, but those two terms are completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic. I remember you mentioning Red Berets. Does the witness wish to change his answer? Because presumably he heard what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We understood each other. It didn't affect his answer. I'm just pointing out the mistake in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... so. So next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where those soldiers were arrested near Crljeni?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this was on the road which is in that area called Put Avnoj, Avnoj Road?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made an oath here that I will speak only about what I saw and heard, not about -- no, not what I heard about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that explosives were placed on the road?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know by whom?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: These activities, these incidents, had they been planned within the framework of the meeting that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the shooting in my village, nothing was planned. There was general confusion, so that if somebody did anything, he did it on his own initiative to protect his own life and that of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: After that, you said that artillery opened fire on the civilians because the men had left towards Bihac.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the artillery started operating, the men still hadn't left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the purpose of the withdrawal of those men towards Bihac?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Because I would have been one of them if I had succeeded. We didn't have a chance, so 90, 95 per cent of those men wouldn't have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the women and children stayed behind, regardless, they were ready for it. Was there a plan to link up with the forces in the Bihac region and come back?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Normally such a plan existed. Whether they would link up then or later on, when the shooting started, in any event the plan was to save lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the ultimatum for the surrender of weapons was actually just an excuse to justify the attack because the demand was that in a few hours several thousand people should be disarmed.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in a few hours, in two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And then you went on to say that there were 400 to 500 pieces of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: 400 to 500 is not several thousand, is it?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you implying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What I am saying is that there's no reason why several hundred people cannot be disarmed in a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a reason; because they were spread out. They were -- there was general confusion. I mentioned that there were ten villages and many hamlets that had all rallied in that one area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you made to the Prosecution on page 10, you said that you had no property and that you easily obtained permission to leave.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I said now. Maybe there's a mistake in the translation. I was living with Mr. Ibrahim Draganovic because of their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sickness, but otherwise I was living in Pudin Han, in my brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the law prescribes how immovable property can be transferred to someone else?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in normal circumstances. But in that republic, there was no rule of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a question, Your Honour. My colleague stated that on page 10 of the statement, Mr. Ticevic stated that it was easy to leave, or that you easily obtained permission to leave. Does he mean that that is actually contained in the statement or that that is his interpretation of it? Because I don't see in the statement that was signed that he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I presume we're talking about the statement of 1st October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's hear Mr. Trbojevic say, because he definitely knows more than you which statement he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Trbojevic, which one, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But which statement? What's the date of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement of the 1st of October, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Page 10, the paragraph before the last, it says that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one but last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "I had no property to sign over but I had to have a certificate from the military that I was not an army conscript. I had to pay 1.400 German marks to Lieutenant Marjanovic. 400 marks went to Marjanovic personally. On the convoy that I was on, there were 20 buses and several trucks. I would estimate that there were over 1.000 non-Serbs who left when I did. I went to Travnik and joined ..." et cetera. He doesn't actually say that he did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say "easily."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if it was, as Mr. Nicholls suggested, that you were drawing conclusions, you have every right to draw that conclusion. I probably would have drawn that conclusion too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make that clear to Your Honours that it was a conclusion, not a statement from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So your question now to -- I think he answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He answered. All right. So go ahead, Mr. Nicholls -- Mr. Trbojevic. I don't want to listen to -- Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1007, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He saw this document a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing this document, the decision on criteria?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The decision contains several rules, shall we call them. I'd like you to look only at the preamble, where it says that, "The War Presidency of the Kljuc municipality, at a session held on the 30th of July, 1992 adopted the following decision ..." Do you agree with me that the War Presidency is not referring to any particular law?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A decision on criteria required in order to move out. That is what it says, but the resettlement was by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that it would have been normal for the Crisis Staff to have said, "Pursuant to Article so and so of law so and so," whereas you don't find that here.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying, and I say again, that there were no rules or laws. They made them as suited them best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: As we are not allowed to enter into any polemics, I will not respond to that comment. When talking about this property, I forgot to mention that in your statement you said that you paid to Lieutenant Marjanovic a certain sum of money while you were collecting documents for moving. And a moment ago you said that you paid something to Tihomir Dakic.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I signed a statement leaving my property for Tihomir Dakic. I had originally wanted to protect Mr. Marjanovic, who assisted me, but you know now and I said that the statement that I signed was for Tihomir Dakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that Tihomir Dakic was a high official where?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kljuc municipality. That is, the Serbian municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were under work duty.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And that this work obligation was assigned to you by someone. I think you used the term "sergeant."

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Bosko Lukic. In my opinion, he was TO commander. And it was implemented by Ratko Marcetic, who was a corporal at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone issue a written document about that work obligation?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that, according to the law on people's defence, it was envisaged which body, under which conditions, in which way war obligations should be assigned?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know anything. We didn't have weapons. And we had to do what they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When you said that in August you saw three men entering Draganovic -- the Draganovic house, you said that this was around midnight.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when it was. I know it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me how you saw them and recognised them in the darkness.

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this was just across the road from where I was sleeping, and the road was lit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And you were able to recognise them going into that house in the dark?

utterances.speaker: NISVET TICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you all the men who were at the checkpoint, and I said that in the evening we would look through the window to watch what people were doing. The house in which the killing occurred is 20 to 30 metres away from the house in which I was sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You see, I am bit by bit learning your language too. I know when you are finished before I get the translation, the interpretation. So I thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. Mr. Nicholls, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ticevic, that brings us to the end of your testimony in this case. I wish to thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and the two Judges, and also on behalf of the Prosecution and the Defence for having come over here, accepted to give evidence. You will now be escorted out of this courtroom by the usher, and the other officers of this Tribunal will take care of you and assist you in your return to your country. I thank you once more. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the next witness comes in, I've received a communique from upstairs, and we'd request that Mr. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ackerman, if he can, tomorrow orally raise his motions rather than waiting to file a release, to give us an idea of what these contain, because if there is going to be any delay in the start of the next witnesses and the next time we're sitting to hear evidence, we need to know it right now, as soon as possible, if we're going to have to make decisions about who comes and when they come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Chuqing, Madam Registrar, could we have the extract of this part communicated to Mr. Ackerman as quickly as possible. In any case, I will be here tomorrow -- we will be here tomorrow. This is why I asked him too. And more or less there is an indication what he may be after, but -- anyway, we'll see. I don't see a reason why -- or at least, I did not catch that in what he was saying that should obstruct the bringing forward of the first witness, at least. But anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just if we can resolve that tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what I would suggest is that when communicating this to Mr. Ackerman, we also indicate -- we also ask of him to indicate to us without delay whether the motion he is contemplating essentially means -- essentially means delaying the bringing over of the first witness. So there at least you know where you stand. In any case, we still have a good week and a half, if not almost two weeks. All right. Next witness is not -- is he protected? Let me -- because this --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's Sanski Most and I need to check. He's not. We just need to make sure that he's not, because I wouldn't like to make such a mistake. Have you checked?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. According to my records, he is -- he is not a protected witness, but -- yes, all right. I just wanted to make sure. Okay. Bring him over, please. Bring him in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Jakov Maric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're here to give evidence in this case. And before you do so, the Rules require me to ask you to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. In other words, you will be making a solemn declaration which is the equivalent of an oath. The text of the solemn declaration is contained on a piece of paper that the usher is going to give you, to hand over to you. And may I now kindly ask you to read that declaration allowed, and that will be your solemn undertaking to this Tribunal that you will be speaking the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. And let mow now explain to you a little bit what's going to happen. You are in a courtroom. That, you have understood. And you are giving evidence in a trial that has been instituted and that has been going on for about ten months already against Radoslav Brdjanin. The procedure that will be followed is a very simple one: To your right, you see a lady standing; that is counsel for the Prosecution. Her name is Ms. Sutherland. I suppose you have already met before today. And she will be conducting the -- what we call the examination-in-chief. It's a series of questions on the basis of which the Prosecution tries to build its case. When the Prosecution finishes with the examination-in-chief, or direct examination, then it will be the turn of the Defence counsel to cross-examine you, to put a series of questions to you. Now, this is a right that the accused has, and it is a fundamental right. So the consequence of this is a very simple one; that you have a duty to answer all questions irrespective of whether they are coming -- irrespective of whether they are being put to you by the Prosecution or by the Defence. You have no right to distinguish between them. You have a duty to answer in as complete a manner as possible and to answer in a way that you will be saying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And with that, I leave you in the hands of Ms. Sutherland, who will start with her first question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Jakov Maric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were born on the 1st of August, 1954?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were born in Sasina in the Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your father's name is Ivo?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Catholic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Ivo, in the Catholic religion, is the patron saint of lawyers. Supposedly he's the only lawyer who made it to saint-hood. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you a Croat?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: A citizen of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You grew up in Sasina. And after completing secondary school, you worked in Zagreb until 1981.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: From 1982 to 1984, you were a member of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You lived abroad between 1984 and 1988.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in 1988, you returned to Bosnia and built a house in Sasina.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You set up a grocery store on the ground floor of your house and ran that business until the 29th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're married and you have two children.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to deal now with the statements that you've provided to authorities. You were interviewed on the 8th of December, 1998 by the Bosnian authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were subsequently interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 11th of March, 2000. Do you recall that interview?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you were visited on the 2nd of June, 2001 by members of the Tribunal, where you signed a Rule 92 declaration.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Besides those statements, the only other statement that you provided to authorities is a very short statement to the UNHCR in Zagreb, prior to immigrating to a third country.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague the other day, you were given an opportunity to review the Bosnian and ICTY statements, and upon review, you wished to make some corrections.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to the Bosnian statement, you stated that one of the guards named in the statement was Zivko Grujicic and that you were unfamiliar with this name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you didn't know how it appeared -- came to appear in the statement. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to a person called Savo, a member of the reserve police force, forcing you to write a letter to your wife in respect of some money, the correction you wished to make to that was the amount of money and that he had forced you to write the amount of 10.000 Deutschmarks and that you provided -- your wife provided him with 10.000 Deutschmarks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Also in the statement, there are a number of names of persons who died as a result of the convoy from Sanski Most to the Manjaca camp on the 7th of July, 1992. Is it correct that you provided some of these names but not all of the names that are contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There was also the name of a person called Darko Matanovic [phoen], otherwise known as Dado, who also died on the convoy and his name was not listed on the statement.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated in relation to those names that the person who -- that the person who took the statement --

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- must have been aware of the other people that had died on the convoy, the names that were included in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: That's right. I have the number of 26 who died; three went missing, and nobody knows anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was it 26 who died on the convoy or 24?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to the ICTY statement provided on the 11th of March, 2000, you wanted to make two corrections to that statement. Where in the statement it said that Sasina was the only Croat village in the Sanski Most municipality, you state that this is incorrect because there are other villages --

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- where the inhabitants are of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Finally, the last correction that you wished to make was in relation to where it states that Serb police arrested over a thousand men in the village of Poljak during their religious holiday Bajram. Is it correct that you don't know the specific number but that it was a large number of men and not just from the village of Poljak but from all over the Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can turn now to events that occurred in the Sanski Most municipality in 1992. The Judges have had an opportunity to hear a great deal of evidence about the political and military developments in the Sanski Most municipality, and I want to focus your testimony on your places of detention and matters relating to your village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, we will be having a break in two minutes' time. I think you've just finished with the corrections --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- section. And may I suggest to you to stop here for the time being and resume immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. 20 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue with the witness, if I can go back to the matter that Mr. Nicholls raised before we broke in relation to the motion that is going to be filed by Defence tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Prosecution wishes to be advised on the particulars to do with that motion, and we would also like to have an oral hearing on it tomorrow or Friday, when we are normally supposed to be sitting in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see, Ms. Sutherland. First of all, I -- don't try to force my hand to force Mr. Ackerman's hand, because I can't force anyone's hand in -- and when -- if and when to file a motion. That's number one. And strictly speaking, I was going perhaps beyond what I should in trying to communicate the transcript to Mr. Ackerman and asking him to give more information than I had actually asked before. I was doing that, knowing that Mr. Ackerman will understand what the preoccupation of the Prosecution is. But beyond that, I'm not prepared to go. I mean, I will not ask Mr. Ackerman to give more information unless he's prepared to do it voluntarily, willingly. I mean, it's just not done. Let's see what Mr. Trbojevic has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we provided the part of today's transcript to Mr. Ackerman at the break, and he told us that tomorrow by 11.00 he will submit the motion and that he's prepared to discuss it after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll wait. We'll see what the motion will be, if it's going to be filed tomorrow by 11.00, and after that, we'll take it up, see if we need -- if we need to summon an urgent sitting, we will do so and meet tomorrow. We had a courtroom booked in any case, so Madam Registrar, I don't think that should be -- there should be any difficulty at all. And if it's necessary to meet tomorrow, we'll meet tomorrow. If it's necessary -- it's not necessary to meet tomorrow, and we can meet the day after or next week, I don't know. Because I haven't seen this motion and I haven't got the least idea what it is about, except very, very generically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's my instructions from Ms. Korner that she would rather deal with this motion orally than in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't say that I would -- we would decide it in writing. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we were to deal with it orally, Ms. Korner would ask if we could sit either Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday next week, if we aren't going to deal with it Thursday or Friday this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sutherland, let's do things as they are normally done. I'll wait until tomorrow, when Mr. Ackerman files this motion. I will have a look at it, see what -- what it is all about, because, for all I know, it might be extremely important or not that important. And if on the face of the document itself it seems that it may require an urgent sitting, we'll sit tomorrow afternoon. So be on the alert, both parties, because if it's necessary, we will sit tomorrow afternoon. And if it's necessary, we will give an oral decision tomorrow afternoon, tomorrow evening. So I don't see any difficulties. But I can't force Mr. Ackerman's hand and say, "No, I want to know beforehand what the motion is all about, what your requests are going to be." I mean, I can't do that. I mean, I asked him very informally earlier on in the day to give us an idea, and he did give a very generic idea on very broad terms. What you can make of that, I don't know. But you can come to various conclusions, actually. I mean, not necessarily one or the other. All right? And we'll take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But anyway, tomorrow morning -- by 11.00 -- if it's filed at 11.00, it should be on my desk by half past 12.00 usually. And then if it's necessary -- I mean, we will all be here tomorrow. And if it's necessary, we will convene a -- an urgent sitting in the afternoon. All right? If it's not that urgent, we will convene Friday or Monday, but please do tell Ms. Korner that we've not been adopting a practice of ignoring the needs of either the Defence or the Prosecution. Okay? So let's go ahead. Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, what villages make up the Sasina local commune? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you move forward a little bit, come near to the microphone, please, because the interpreters can't hear you well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Skrljevita, Kladernica, Razboj, Gornje Selo and Dragoc.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And approximately how many people live in these four villages?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: According to the pre-war census, it was 3.236 -- 3.636.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of these people?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Mostly Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the day of the takeover of power by the Serbs in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After this date, were the non-Serb population ordered to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Of course. They went from village to village through Mahala, Trnova, Sasina, Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "they," who are you referring to? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: The Serb police or army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you become aware that you had to surrender the weapons?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: It was broadcast over the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you possess a weapon?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: A civilian pistol, registered with the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you surrender that weapon?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there any armed resistance in your village of Sasina?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was your freedom of movement restricted in any way after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Totally. It was completely restricted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were there any demands made on the radio?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: To hand over weapons and for the surrender of the villagers by placing a white sheet on each house as a sign of surrender to the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who made these demands?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: The Serbs demanded it over the Serb radio station of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the religious holiday Bajram in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the exact date?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Not the exact date. Maybe it was May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Mass arrests of non-Serb citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where from?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: From all the villages in the area of Sanski Most. Mostly Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know where the people were taken after they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Those who were registered as extremists by the Serb authorities were taken to the police station --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not get the rest of the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, the interpreter had difficulty in following you, and they could only understand the first part of your answer. Could you answer the same question again, please. The question was: Do you know where the people were taken after they were arrested? And you had started saying: Those who were registered as extremists by the Serb authorities were taken to the police station. Then you said something else, but it was not picked up by the -- not picked up by the interpreters. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those registered as extremists by the Serb police, according to them, were taken to the Betonirka prison and other prisons in smaller schools and also to the Krings factory and to some other halls.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was the village of Sasina shelled?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: A smaller area, in the area of Trnova.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when this happened?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: In late May and early June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know from what direction the shelling came?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: It was mortar fire, so it was very difficult to determine the direction. It was either from Usorci or from Sana.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the people that live in those two areas?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: The area from where there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Serb nationality. The village of Usorci and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name of the second village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the name of the second village -- the first one was Usorci. And the second one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dabar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dabar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, I would just ask you to try and keep your voice up so that the interpreters can hear your answers. Were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: On the 20th -- on the 20th of June at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said the --

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: The 29th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 29th.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: The 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: The Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of the people from the Serb police who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Gojko Macura, Krunic Milorad, Zdravko Papric [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: The reason was for me to just provide a brief statement, and then I would be released. I was taken to Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where is Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: Not far from the Sanski Most police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was a statement taken from you?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV MARIC
utterances.text: On the third day I was interrogated by the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long were you detained in Betonirka?
